name: Hinterrhein in the Domleschg
summary: The canton of Graubünden put the Hinterrhein in the Domleschg into one straight bed, filled the old gravel bed with silt to make farmland, and tamed the Nolla torrent above Thusis.

stops.title: A dam through the gravel
text: Before 1832 the Hinterrhein spread over the whole valley floor between Thusis and Rothenbrunnen. It ran in many arms over gravel. Floods often covered the meadows of the Domleschg.

In 1832 work started on the plan of the cantonal engineer Richard La Nicca. A long dam on the east side held the river in one straight bed. The map of 1859 shows the work half done: the new straight river on the east, and west of it the wide old bed (red area).

lines.name: Hinterrhein today, in the straight bed of 1832-1892 (OpenStreetMap)

areas.name: Wide old gravel bed of the Hinterrhein, west of the new dam (map of 1859)

stops.title: The Nolla fights back
text: The Nolla is a torrent (a steep mountain stream) that joins the Rhine at Thusis. In big storms it brought mud and stones. Its debris dammed the Rhine above Thusis up to 12 m high. When the dam broke, a flood wave ran down the Domleschg.

In 1868, 1869 and 1870 the Nolla did this three times and damaged the new Rhine works. From 1870 workers built a row of stone check dams (walls across the bed) in the Nolla gorge. The blue line west of Thusis is the Nolla.

lines.name: Hinterrhein today, in the straight bed of 1832-1892 (OpenStreetMap)
Nolla today, the torrent with its check dams (OpenStreetMap)

areas.name: Wide old gravel bed of the Hinterrhein, west of the new dam (map of 1859)

stops.title: Silt makes new fields
text: La Nicca did not leave the old gravel bed empty. He cut it into fields with low cross dams. Through a gate at Thusis he let in the muddy water of the Nolla. The mud settled and slowly raised the ground. This is called colmation (filling land with river silt).
On the new land the canton opened the institution of Realta in 1855, a work and detention home. The Rhine work was finished in 1892. The red area shows where the old bed was.

lines.name: Hinterrhein today, in the straight bed of 1832-1892 (OpenStreetMap)
Nolla today, the torrent with its check dams (OpenStreetMap)

areas.name: Wide old gravel bed of the Hinterrhein, west of the new dam (map of 1859)

stops.title: Fields where the river was
text: Today the Hinterrhein runs in its straight bed of 1892 (blue). The fields, the motorway A13 and the Realta buildings lie on the old gravel bed (red).
The work on the Nolla never ended. The canton still repairs and replaces the old check dams.

lines.name: Hinterrhein today, in the straight bed of 1832-1892 (OpenStreetMap)
Nolla today, the torrent with its check dams (OpenStreetMap)

areas.name: Wide old gravel bed of the Hinterrhein, west of the new dam (map of 1859)

notes: The red area is traced on the Dufour-type map of 1859, which already shows the new east dam; the bed before 1832 is not on any map in this series. HLS dates the start to 1832 (Rhein, La Nicca) but the HLS article on Realta says dyke works began in 1830. The Nolla is only drawn as today's course: the check dams changed its bed height, not its route. The extent of the colmation fields is approximate.
why: The Hinterrhein in the Domleschg had a wide gravel bed with many arms. The Nolla torrent at Thusis made it worse: it dumped mud and stones into the Rhine, dammed it up to 12 m high, and then the water broke out over the valley. Escher of the Linth already wrote about the Nolla after the flood of 1807.

Richard La Nicca, the first cantonal engineer of Graubünden, made the plan in 1826. Work began in 1832. Dams held the river in one bed from Cazis to Rothenbrunnen, and silt from the Nolla filled the old bed to make farmland. The floods of 1868 to 1870 showed that the Rhine was not safe while the Nolla was wild. So from 1870 the canton, with money from the Confederation, built big stone check dams in the Nolla gorge under the engineers Adolf and Friedrich von Salis. By 1910 there were about 20 large and 46 smaller dams.
The Rhine work was finished in 1892. The Nolla never stopped moving: slopes in its catchment keep slipping, and the canton still renews the old dams today.

name: Werdenberg inland canal
stretch: Trübbach (Wartau) to Rüthi, beside the Alpine Rhine
summary: St. Gallen dug a canal on the land side of the new Rhine dams to collect the side streams, so that the dams had no gaps and the marshes of the Werdenberg plain could be drained.

stops.title: Streams and marsh
text: Around 1860 the plain between Sevelen and Sennwald was wet. Many streams came down from the mountains and wandered over the plain to the Rhine. Between Gams and Haag lay a large marsh, the Riet (red area).
Next to the Rhine ran old side arms such as the Buchser Giessen (red line). When the Rhine was high, its water pushed back into these streams and flooded the fields.

lines.name: Buchser Giessen, an old side stream next to the Rhine (map of 1860)

areas.name: Wet meadows and marsh (Riet) between Sax, Gams, Haag and Grabs (map of 1860)

stops.title: A canal beside the dams
text: From 1862 the Rhine got high dams. But where a stream entered the Rhine, the dam had a gap. So from 1882 to 1886 workers dug the Werdenberg inland canal (blue) on the land side of the dams. It takes the streams and leads them to the Rhine near Rüthi.

Most of the earth was dug by hand. Small trains carried it away. Now the water level on the plain could drop. In 1885-1887 the first large land drainage of Switzerland started near Haag, on the old marsh.

lines.name: Werdenberg inland canal (built 1882-1886, OpenStreetMap)
Buchser Giessen, an old side stream next to the Rhine (map of 1860)

areas.name: Wet meadows and marsh (Riet) between Sax, Gams, Haag and Grabs (map of 1860)

stops.title: Farmland and a green canal
text: Today the canal (blue) still runs for about 21 km beside the Rhine. The old marsh (red) is farmland, with the A13 motorway and villages on it.
Before the canal, the Rhine dams had gaps where streams came in. Now the dams are closed along the whole valley.

lines.name: Werdenberg inland canal (built 1882-1886, OpenStreetMap)

areas.name: Wet meadows and marsh (Riet) between Sax, Gams, Haag and Grabs (map of 1860)

notes: HLS gives 1882-1886; Vischer says the canal was finished in 1886 and shows a photo of the work at Salez about 1882. The length (c. 21 km) is measured on OpenStreetMap. The marsh outline is traced roughly on the 1860 map (hatching of wet meadows); the area that was drained was larger.
why: Before the Rhine was corrected, more than 30 streams flowed into the Alpine Rhine below Landquart. The Rhine bed rose with gravel, so in high water the Rhine pushed back into these streams. The plain stayed wet, and in the floods of 1817-1890 the villages lost their harvest again and again.

From 1862 St. Gallen built high dams along the Rhine, with one third of the cost paid by the Confederation. The dams needed to be closed. The engineer Jost Wey therefore built the inland canal in 1882-1886 to collect the side streams and bring them to the Rhine further down. The canal network then made land drainage possible, starting at Haag in 1885-1887.
The gain was new farmland. The loss was the wet meadows and marshes of the valley: HLS counts 6039 ha of valley marsh in 1890 and only 106 ha in 1999.

name: Rheintal inland canal
stretch: Sennwald to St. Margrethen (into the Old Rhine)
summary: As part of the international Rhine regulation, Switzerland dug a canal through the lower St. Gallen Rhine valley that collects the side streams and drains the plain into the Old Rhine.

stops.title: A wet valley floor
text: In 1891 the plain between Oberriet, Altstätten and Widnau was full of wet meadows and peat (red area). The streams from the hills ended in this plain or ran to the Rhine through many ditches.
The Rhine then still made its big loop around Diepoldsau and ran to Lake Constance near Altenrhein.

areas.name: Wet meadows and marsh between Oberriet, Altstätten and Widnau (map of 1891)

stops.title: One canal for all streams
text: In 1892 Switzerland and Austria signed a treaty to regulate the Rhine. The Rhine got a new mouth at Fussach in 1900. Its old bed from St. Margrethen to the lake became free.

From 1896 to 1906 Switzerland dug the Rheintal inland canal (blue). It starts at Sennwald, collects the side streams and flows into the Old Rhine at St. Margrethen. The peat made the work hard and expensive.

lines.name: Rheintal inland canal (built 1896-1906, OpenStreetMap)

areas.name: Wet meadows and marsh between Oberriet, Altstätten and Widnau (map of 1891)

stops.title: Drained plain
text: Today the canal (blue) drains the whole plain. The old wet meadows (red) are fields, roads and industrial zones.
In 1999 and 2013 heavy rain brought more water than the canal could take, and parts of Widnau and Rüthi were flooded.

lines.name: Rheintal inland canal (built 1896-1906, OpenStreetMap)

areas.name: Wet meadows and marsh between Oberriet, Altstätten and Widnau (map of 1891)

notes: HLS gives 1895-1906, the canal association gives 1894-1906 (preliminary works at Monstein 1894-1895, canal 1896-1906). Length c. 22 km is measured on OpenStreetMap (the upper part is named "Rheintaler Binnenkanal", the lower part "Binnenkanal"). The marsh outline is a rough trace of the hatched wet meadows on the 1891 map. Check the 1916 map: the canal should be visible there.
why: The lower Rhine valley was flat and wet. Floods of the Rhine in 1868 in the St. Gallen Rhine valley and 1890 in Vorarlberg led Switzerland and Austria to sign the treaty of 1892 on the international Rhine regulation.

The treaty made the Fussach cut (1900) and the Diepoldsau cut (1923). Each country had to build the side canals on its own bank. On the Swiss side this was the Rheintal inland canal, built under the engineer Jost Wey. Because the Rhine now ran to Fussach, the canal could use the old Rhine bed below St. Margrethen as its outlet.

The canal made land drainage possible and turned the marshes into farmland. Later it needed drop structures at Lienz, Blatten and Montlingen, which also make electricity. Today the area is built up, and floods in 1999 and 2013 showed that the canal is now too small in places.

name: Landquart in the Prättigau
stretch: Schiers to Grüsch (and down to the Rhine)
summary: Dams and silt filling from 1870, and a straight canal built in 1912-1918, took the wide gravel bed of the Landquart between Schiers and Grüsch and turned it into farmland.

stops.title: A valley of gravel
text: Between Schiers and Grüsch the Landquart had a very wide bed with many arms and big sand and gravel banks (red area). The red line is the main channel on the map of 1865.
Floods of the Landquart and its side streams did great damage in 1464 and 1762.

lines.name: Main channel of the Landquart before the correction (map of 1865)

areas.name: Wide gravel bed of the Landquart between Schiers and Grüsch (map of 1865)

stops.title: A narrow straight canal
text: From 1870 the communes built protective dams and let the muddy river water settle on low land to raise it (colmation). Until 1900 this gained about 200 ha of farmland in the valley.
After the floods of 1910, the Landquart between Schiers and Grüsch was put into a narrow straight canal from 1912 to 1918 (blue). The old gravel banks became fields.

lines.name: Landquart today, in the straight canal of 1912-1918 (OpenStreetMap)
Main channel of the Landquart before the correction (map of 1865)

areas.name: Wide gravel bed of the Landquart between Schiers and Grüsch (map of 1865)

stops.title: Room for the river again
text: The narrow canal made the water faster. The river dug into its bed, and plants and fish lost their habitat.
From 2008 to 2011 the canton made the bed wider again at four places near Schiers and Grüsch, each 300 to 900 m long. The blue line is the river today; the red area shows how wide it once was.

lines.name: Landquart today, in the straight canal of 1912-1918 (OpenStreetMap)
Main channel of the Landquart before the correction (map of 1865)

areas.name: Wide gravel bed of the Landquart between Schiers and Grüsch (map of 1865)

notes: HLS gives the floods (1464, 1762, 1910, 1927) and "from 1870 protective works and colmation, c. 2 million m2 by 1900" for the whole valley. The canton gives 1912-1918 for the canal between Schiers and Grüsch. That the 1910 flood triggered the 1912 canal is my reading of the dates, not stated in a source. The positions of the four widening sites are approximate. The old line and area are traced on the Dufour-type map of 1865 and may be off by 50-100 m.
why: The Landquart comes down from the Silvretta and brings much gravel. In the open part of the Prättigau, between Schiers and Grüsch, it spread over the valley floor in many arms. Floods in 1464, 1762, 1910 and 1927 did heavy damage.

From 1870 the communes and the canton built dams and colmation works (fields filled with river silt). The canal of 1912-1918 then fixed the river in one narrow bed. It gave farmland and protection, and it helped the economy of the valley.

Later engineers saw the downside: in the narrow bed the water ran faster and dug the bed deeper, and the river lost its natural banks. So in 2008-2011 the canton widened the river again at four places.

name: Thur in the Toggenburg
summary: St. Gallen straightened and dammed the upper Thur between Ebnat-Kappel and Lichtensteig, so that the flat valley floor at Wattwil could be farmed and built on.

stops.title: Loops below Wattwil
text: Around 1900 the Thur made loops and wide gravel banks in the flat valley floor between Ulisbach and Wattwil (red line). The low land beside the river was poorly protected and often flooded.
The railway already ran along the west side of the valley, close to the river.

lines.name: Thur before the correction, with its loops near Wattwil (map of 1900)

stops.title: A straight Thur
text: From 1907 to 1913 the canton of St. Gallen corrected the Thur between Ebnat-Kappel and Lichtensteig. Workers cut off the loops and built dams. The river now runs in a straight bed (blue).
The engineer Arnold Sonderegger drew the plans for the work at Wattwil. The valley floor could now be used more intensively.

lines.name: Thur today (OpenStreetMap)
Thur before the correction, with its loops near Wattwil (map of 1900)

stops.title: Houses on the old bed
text: Today the Thur still follows the straight bed of 1913 (blue). Streets, factories and sports fields of Wattwil lie where the loops were (red).

lines.name: Thur today (OpenStreetMap)
Thur before the correction, with its loops near Wattwil (map of 1900)

notes: HLS (Thur, Wattwil) gives 1907-1913; the St. Gallen state archive and Wikipedia say 1907-1914. The name of Arnold Sonderegger comes from the state archive catalogue (plans for the Thur regulation at Wattwil). Between Ebnat-Kappel and Ulisbach the old and new courses are almost the same on the maps, so only the Wattwil stretch (Lichtensteig to Ulisbach) is drawn in red. Wikipedia mentions a second correction in 1983; not confirmed in a high-trust source, so not used.
why: The upper Thur is a mountain river with sudden floods. In the flat valley floor around Wattwil it made loops and moved its gravel banks. The fields next to it were poorly protected.

Further down, Thurgau and Zurich had corrected the Thur in 1874-1893. In 1907-1913 the canton of St. Gallen followed with its own correction between Ebnat-Kappel and Lichtensteig. The aim was flood protection and more usable land on the valley floor.
The straight bed made room for Wattwil to grow onto the valley floor. The price was the loss of the natural river banks.

name: Inn and Flaz at Samedan
stretch: Punt Muragl and Samedan to Bever (Inn up to Zuoz)
summary: The Inn in the Upper Engadine was put between dikes at the end of the 19th century, the Flaz and Inn at Samedan were squeezed into a closed canal after the floods of 1951 and 1954, and in 2004 the Flaz got a new 4 km bed away from the village.

stops.title: Two rivers meet at the village
text: At Samedan two rivers meet: the Inn from the lakes of St. Moritz, and the Flaz from the Bernina glaciers. On the map of 1878 the Flaz crosses the plain from Punt Muragl and joins the Inn at the bridge of Samedan (red line).
The Inn flooded the Upper Engadine many times, for example in 1566. At the end of the 19th century it was corrected between Samedan and Zuoz. From then on dikes protected the village.

lines.name: Flaz in 1878: from Punt Muragl across the plain to the Inn at Samedan (map of 1878)
Inn (En) between dikes (OpenStreetMap)

stops.title: Squeezed into a canal
text: In 1951 and 1954 big floods hit Samedan. After them, the dikes were raised and the Flaz and the Inn were forced into a closed canal along the village (red line and Inn).
The village now lay next to two high dikes. If they broke, the water would flow into the houses.

lines.name: Flaz before 2004: its canal along the west side of the plain to the Inn at Samedan (map of 2001)
Inn (En) between dikes (OpenStreetMap)

stops.title: A new bed for the Flaz
text: In July 1987 only about 20 cm were missing before the water would have run over the dikes. The canton then told Samedan to build better protection by 2005.

In April 2004 the Flaz was moved into a new 4 km bed (blue) through the Champagna plain, east of the airfield. It now joins the Inn below the village. The old canal (red) was removed, and a part of the Inn got a natural bed again. The work cost 29.6 million francs.

lines.name: Flaz before 2004: its canal along the west side of the plain to the Inn at Samedan (map of 2001)
New course of the Flaz through the Champagna plain (2002-2005, OpenStreetMap)
Inn (En) between dikes (OpenStreetMap)

notes: HLS (Inn) says only "end of the 19th century, corrected between Samedan and Zuoz"; no exact years found. The maps of 1878 and 1900 differ little near Samedan, so no separate old Inn line is drawn. The Flaz of 1878 is traced on the map of 1878; the Flaz canal (stops 2 and 3) is traced on the map of 2001. Both run along the west side of the plain to the Inn at Samedan. The cost is 29.6 million francs on the canton page and 28.4 million in the canton project sheet; the month April 2004 is from the project sheet. 1566 and 1951 floods are from HLS, 1954 from the canton.
why: Samedan lies where the Flaz meets the Inn. Both rivers can bring a lot of water at the same time, from rain and from melting snow and glaciers. The Inn flooded the Upper Engadine in 1566, 1951 and other years.

At the end of the 19th century the Inn was corrected between Samedan and Zuoz, and dikes were built around the village. After the floods of 1951 and 1954 the dikes were raised and both rivers were squeezed into a closed canal. This made the village safe from small floods, but a dike break would have been a disaster, as the near miss of July 1987 showed.

Instead of raising the dikes again, Samedan and the canton chose a new solution: in 2002-2005 the Flaz was moved away from the village into a new bed through the plain, with 75% of the money from the Confederation and the canton. It was the first relocation of a larger Swiss river in more than 80 years, and it also gave new habitat to plants and animals. Downstream, the Inn near Bever was given a natural bed again in two stages until 2020.

name: Vedeggio at Agno
stretch: Bioggio to the delta at Agno (Lake Lugano)
summary: From 1906 the Vedeggio was taken out of its winding bed through Agno and put into a straight canal across the Piano d'Agno, which made the plain usable for farms and later for the airport of Lugano.

stops.title: A river through the village
text: In 1905 the Vedeggio ran down the west side of the plain in a wide bed with gravel banks (red line). It passed close to Agno and reached Lake Lugano west of the village.
The plain, the Piano d'Agno, was wet and partly marshy. People had started to drain it already in the 19th century.

lines.name: Vedeggio before the correction, through Agno village (map of 1905)

stops.title: A straight canal
text: The correction of the Vedeggio started in 1906. The river got a new, straight bed in the middle of the plain (blue). It now reaches the lake east of Agno.
The plain was now dry enough for fields. In 1938 an airfield with a 1 km runway opened on it.

lines.name: Vedeggio today, in its straight canal to Lake Lugano (OpenStreetMap)
Vedeggio before the correction, through Agno village (map of 1905)

stops.title: Airport and industry
text: Today the Vedeggio still runs in its straight canal (blue). The plain is full of the airport of Lugano-Agno, roads and industry.
The canton is now raising the dikes of the lower Vedeggio again, to protect Agno, Bioggio and Muzzano from a 100-year flood.

lines.name: Vedeggio today, in its straight canal to Lake Lugano (OpenStreetMap)
Vedeggio before the correction, through Agno village (map of 1905)

notes: HLS (Agno) gives only the start (1906) of the Vedeggio correction and says the drainage of the Piano d'Agno began in the 19th century; the end year is unknown. The map of 1934 already shows the straight canal. The 1938 airfield date is from a Federal Administrative Court ruling. The old line is traced on the map of 1905 and only covers Bioggio to the lake.
why: Flat land is rare in Ticino. The Piano d'Agno, at the mouth of the Vedeggio into Lake Lugano, was wet and the river moved over its gravel banks. Drainage of the plain had started in the 19th century.
In 1906 the correction of the Vedeggio began. The river was put into a straight canal, and the drained plain gave the commune of Agno much more productive land, first for farming.
After 1945 the plain filled with industry, shops and the airport of Lugano. Today the canton, the Confederation and the communes pay for new flood protection on the lower Vedeggio.

name: Alpine Rhine from Chur to the Tardis bridge
stretch: Chur (Plessur mouth) to the Tardis bridge near Landquart
summary: After the flood of 1868, Graubünden built dams along the Rhine from Chur to the Tardis bridge, so that the wide gravel bed near Untervaz and Trimmis became a narrow river.

stops.title: Gravel banks near Untervaz
text: Around 1859 the Rhine between Chur and the Tardis bridge had a wide gravel bed with several arms (red area). Near Untervaz and Trimmis it was up to a few hundred metres wide.
The railway from Rorschach to Chur, opened in 1858, ran just beside the river on the east side.

areas.name: Wide gravel bed of the Rhine near Untervaz (map of 1859)

stops.title: One bed between dams
text: In 1868 a great flood hit the Alpine Rhine. After it, the engineer Richard La Nicca led the correction from Chur to the Tardis bridge. Dams now hold the Rhine in one bed (blue).
The work was finished in 1892, together with the Hinterrhein work in the Domleschg. The old gravel banks (red) became meadows and woods.

lines.name: Rhine today, between the dams of 1868-1892 (OpenStreetMap)

areas.name: Wide gravel bed of the Rhine near Untervaz (map of 1859)

stops.title: Motorway on the gravel
text: Today the A13 motorway, the railway and gravel works lie on the old river bed. The Rhine (blue) runs in the bed of 1892.
Below the Tardis bridge the St. Gallen Rhine correction of 1860-1890 continues the straight river to Lake Constance.

lines.name: Rhine today, between the dams of 1868-1892 (OpenStreetMap)

areas.name: Wide gravel bed of the Rhine near Untervaz (map of 1859)

notes: HLS says the correction between Chur and the Tardis bridge was realised by La Nicca after the flood of 1868 and finished in 1892; it gives no start year, so "1868" in built is the flood year. La Nicca was then over 70 and no longer cantonal engineer (he left that post in 1853), so his exact role is unclear. The gravel bed is traced on the Dufour-type map of 1859.
why: Above Landquart the Alpine Rhine carries the gravel of the Vorder- and Hinterrhein, the Plessur and many torrents. Between Chur and the Tardis bridge it spread over a wide gravel bed. The railway of 1858 and the villages of Trimmis and Untervaz lay close to it.
The great flood of 1868 hit many parts of Switzerland, also the Rhine valley. It started the correction from Chur to the Tardis bridge, led by Richard La Nicca, and finished in 1892.

The dams protected the railway, the road and the farmland. The river lost its wide gravel bed and floodplain forests. Since 1995 an international commission of the cantons, Liechtenstein, Vorarlberg and the two states coordinates all work on the Alpine Rhine.
